title: Keeping old buildings, or building new ones

turns.speaker: Dario
turns.text: They want to demolish the sixties library and put up something six storeys taller. The listing application went in yesterday.

turns.speaker: Nell
turns.text: People will fight for that building now purely because someone wants it gone. Nobody liked it in 2005.

turns.speaker: Imogen
turns.text: That's true of almost every period. Victorian buildings were being knocked down as eyesores within living memory.

turns.speaker: Dario
turns.text: So the rule is wait forty years and see?

turns.speaker: Imogen
turns.text: Roughly, yes. Taste has a cycle and demolition doesn't reverse.

turns.speaker: Nell
turns.text: The carbon argument is the stronger one now anyway. About a third of a building's whole lifetime emissions are in the construction itself.

turns.speaker: Nell
turns.text: Roughly, for a modern one. So knocking down a sound building to put up an efficient one can take fifty years to break even.

turns.speaker: Imogen
turns.text: By which point the new one is due for replacement.

turns.speaker: Dario
turns.text: The counter is density. Six more storeys is housing for people who currently live forty miles away and drive in.

turns.speaker: Nell
turns.text: That's real, and it's the argument that should be made rather than the efficiency one.

turns.speaker: Imogen
turns.text: Retrofit usually beats both, and it's unglamorous, so it loses to whoever has a rendering.

turns.speaker: Dario
turns.text: Nobody ever won a council vote with a picture of new insulation.

points: A 1960s library faces demolition for a taller replacement, prompting a listing application.
Nell and Imogen note taste runs in cycles, with Victorian buildings once demolished as eyesores, so delay is prudent because demolition is irreversible.
Nell cites embodied carbon: roughly a third of a modern building's lifetime emissions come from construction.
Replacing a sound building with an efficient one can therefore take around fifty years to break even.
Dario's strongest argument is density, housing people who currently commute long distances.
They agree retrofit usually outperforms both options but loses politically because it is unglamorous.
